**Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo** ([/æ ˈ k ʊ f oʊ ɑː ˈ d oʊ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/8/83/En-Nana_Akufo-Addo.oga/En-Nana_Akufo-Addo.oga.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-Nana_Akufo-Addo.oga "File:En-Nana Akufo-Addo.oga")[_a-KUUF-oh ah-DOH_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-OL_Elected_President_of_Ghana-1) born 29 March 1944) is a Ghanaian politician who served as the 13th [president of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Ghana "President of Ghana") from January 2017 to January 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-citinewsroom.com-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-5) He previously served as [Attorney General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attorney_General_of_Ghana "Attorney General of Ghana") from 2001 to 2003 and as [Minister for Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Foreign_Affairs_(Ghana) "Minister for Foreign Affairs (Ghana)") from 2003 to 2007 under the administration of then-president [John Kufuor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kufuor "John Kufuor").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-6)

Akufo-Addo first ran for president in the year [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Ghanaian_general_election "2008 Ghanaian general election") and again in [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Ghanaian_presidential_election "2012 Ghanaian presidential election"), both times as the presidential candidate of the [New Patriotic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Patriotic_Party "New Patriotic Party") (NPP). He lost on both occasions to [National Democratic Congress'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Congress_(Ghana) "National Democratic Congress (Ghana)") candidates: [John Evans Atta Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Evans_Atta_Mills "John Evans Atta Mills") in 2008 and [John Dramani Mahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama "John Dramani Mahama") in 2012. After the 2012 general elections, he refused to concede and proceeded to court to challenge the electoral results, but the [Supreme Court of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Ghana "Supreme Court of Ghana") affirmed Mahama's victory.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-7)

He was chosen as the presidential candidate of the New Patriotic Party for a third time for the [2016 general elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Ghanaian_general_election "2016 Ghanaian general election"), and this time he defeated incumbent [John Dramani Mahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mahama "John Mahama") in the first round, winning with 53.85% of the votes. This marked the first time in a Ghanaian presidential history that an opposition candidate won an outright majority in the first round.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-8) It was the first time that an opposition candidate had unseated an incumbent president. Akuffo-Addo again secured an outright majority in the first round of the [2020 general elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Ghanaian_general_election "2020 Ghanaian general election") (winning with 51.59% of the vote), defeating Mahama for a second time.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-nanare-elected-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-11)

Akufo-Addo's government initially drew broad popularity from the Ghanaian public, promoting a nationalistic "Ghana Beyond Aid" agenda.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-12) The latter part of his tenure, however, was marked with the worst financial crises in Ghana in a generation, with inflation reaching up to 40% in both 2022 and 2023.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-15) His government attributed this to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") and [Russian invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russian invasion of Ukraine"), but many observers pointed to mismanagement of public funds.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-18) Because he was [term-limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Term_limit "Term limit"), he peacefully handed over power to the NDC's Mahama on 7 January 2025 after the incumbent NPP lost power amid the unpopularity of his administration.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo was born in Accra, Ghana, on March 29, 1944, to [Adeline Ofori-Atta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adeline_Akufo-Addo "Adeline Akufo-Addo") and [Edward Akufo-Addo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Akufo-Addo "Edward Akufo-Addo").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-New_African-20) His father, Edward Akufo-Addo, from [Akropong-Akuapem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akropong-Akuapem "Akropong-Akuapem") was Ghana's third [Chief Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_Ghana "Chief Justice of Ghana") from 1966 to 1970, [chairman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairperson "Chairperson") of the 1967–68 [Constitutional Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Commission "Constitutional Commission") and the non-executive president of Ghana from 1970 till 1972.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-New_African-20) Akufo-Addo's maternal grandfather was [Nana Sir Ofori Atta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Sir_Ofori_Atta "Nana Sir Ofori Atta"), King of [Akyem Abuakwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akyem_Abuakwa "Akyem Abuakwa"), who was a member of the Executive Council of the Gold Coast before Ghana's independence.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-New_African-20) He is a nephew of ex-Speaker of Parliament [Kofi Asante Ofori-Atta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Asante_Ofori-Atta "Kofi Asante Ofori-Atta") and the Big Six member [William Ofori Atta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ofori_Atta "William Ofori Atta"). [J. B. Danquah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._B._Danquah "J. B. Danquah"), another member of [The Big Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Big_Six_(Ghana) "The Big Six (Ghana)"), was a granduncle of his.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-21)

He started his primary education at the Government Boys School and Rowe Road School (now Kinbu), both in Accra Central.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-22) He went to [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") and continued his education at [Holmewood House Preparatory School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmewood_House_School "Holmewood House School") before studying for his O-Level and A-Level examinations at [Lancing College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancing_College "Lancing College"), [Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex "Sussex"), where he was nicknamed "Billy" and joined the Anglican faith.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-OL_Elected_President_of_Ghana-1) He began the [Philosophy, Politics and Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy,_Politics_and_Economics "Philosophy, Politics and Economics") course at [New College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_College,_Oxford "New College, Oxford"), in 1962, but left soon afterwards.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-23) He returned to Ghana in 1962 to teach at the [Accra Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra_Academy "Accra Academy"), before going to read economics at the [University of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana "University of Ghana"), [Legon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legon "Legon"), in 1964, earning a BSc (Econ) degree in 1967.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-24) He subsequently joined the [Middle Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Temple "Middle Temple") and trained as a lawyer under the apprenticeship system known as the [Inns of Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inns_of_Court "Inns of Court"), where no formal law degree was required.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-25) He was called to the English Bar (Middle Temple) in July 1971. He was called to the Ghanaian bar in July 1975.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-Ivor-26) Akufo-Addo worked with the [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") office of the U.S. law firm [Coudert Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coudert_Brothers "Coudert Brothers"). In 1979, he co-founded the law firm Akufo-Addo, Prempeh and Co.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-27)

## Political career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Political career")]

Though known by his friends to have been a vocal supporter of the [Convention People's Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_People's_Party "Convention People's Party") (CPP) while a student in the [University of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana "University of Ghana"), he switched sides to the rival [United Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Party_(Ghana) "United Party (Ghana)") (UP) tradition following the overthrow of President [Kwame Nkrumah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah "Kwame Nkrumah") in 1966 after which his father, Edward Akufo-Addo became ceremonial president of Ghana in 1969. Akufo-Addo's participation in politics formally began in the late 1970s when he joined the People's Movement for Freedom and Justice (PMFJ),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-daily_graphic-28) an organization formed to oppose the General [Acheampong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignatius_Kutu_Acheampong "Ignatius Kutu Acheampong")-led Supreme Military Council's Union Government proposals.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-ansah-29) In May 1995, he was among a broad group of elites who formed Alliance for Change, an alliance that organized demonstrations against Neo-liberal policies such as the introduction of [Value Added Tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_Added_Tax "Value Added Tax") and human rights violations of the [Rawlings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Rawlings "Jerry Rawlings") presidency. At the forefront of this demonstration were himself, [Abdul Malik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdul_Malik "Abdul Malik"), [Kwaku Baako](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kweku_Baako_Jnr "Kweku Baako Jnr") and Saifullah Senior minister [Victor Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Newman_(politician) "Victor Newman (politician)"), [Kwasi Pratt Jnr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwesi_Pratt_Jnr "Kwesi Pratt Jnr"), Dr. [Charles Wereko Brobbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Wereko-Brobby "Charles Wereko-Brobby") among others. They were joined by about 100,000 other people. The protest was named "[Kume Preko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kume_Preko "Kume Preko")".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-31) As an elite, Akufo-Addo vied for leadership positions; the broad-based opposition alliance eventually fell apart.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-Ivor-26) In the 1990s, he formed a civil rights organization called Ghana's Committee on Human and People's Rights.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-daily_graphic-28)

He was a member of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th parliament of the 4th republic representing the [Abuakwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuakwa "Abuakwa") constituency.

In the 1996 elections, he polled 28,526 votes out of the 50,263 valid votes cast representing 56.75% over [Owuraku Amofah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owuraku_Amofah "Owuraku Amofah") who polled 20,173 votes, Adoo-Aikins who polled 705 votes, Ahmadu Rufai who polled 682 votes and Emmanuel Kofi Tamakloe who polled 177 votes.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-32) He won again in the 2000 General Elections with 28,633 votes out of the 45,795 valid votes cast representing 62.50% over Christiana Annor who polled 14,486 votes, Addo-Aikins who polled 1,088 votes, Theresa Stella Amakye who polled 593 votes, Kofi Opoku-Gyamera who polled 519 votes and Isaac Duodu Awah who also polled 506 votes.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-34)

### Presidential bids

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Presidential bids")]

In October 1998, Akufo-Addo competed for the a presidential run of the [NPP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Patriotic_Party "New Patriotic Party")[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-Ivor-26) and lost to [John Kufuor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kufuor "John Kufuor"), who subsequently won the December 2000 presidential election and assumed office as President of Ghana in January 2001. Akufo-Addo was the chief campaigner for Kufuor in the 2000 election. He became the first attorney general and Minister for justice of the Kufuor era, and later moved to the [Ministry of Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_for_Foreign_Affairs_(Ghana) "Minister for Foreign Affairs (Ghana)") and [New Partnership for Africa's Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Partnership_for_Africa's_Development "New Partnership for Africa's Development") (NEPAD).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-36)

In 2007, he was the popular candidate tipped to win the [New Patriotic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Patriotic_Party "New Patriotic Party")'s presidential primaries.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-37) In 2008, Akufo-Addo represented the NPP in a closely [contested election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Ghanaian_general_election "2008 Ghanaian general election") against [John Atta Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Atta_Mills "John Atta Mills") of NDC.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-38) In the first round of voting, Akufo-Addo tallied 49.13%, leading Atta Mills with a slim margin that was below the constitutional threshold of 50% to become the outright winner.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-Gabby-39)

Akufo-Addo ran again as the [NPP's presidential candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Ghanaian_New_Patriotic_Party_presidential_primary_election "2010 Ghanaian New Patriotic Party presidential primary election") in the [2012 national elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Ghanaian_general_election "2012 Ghanaian general election") against [NDC's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Congress_(Ghana) "National Democratic Congress (Ghana)")[John Mahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mahama "John Mahama"), successor to the late Atta Mills. Mahama was declared the winner of the election, an outcome that was legally challenged by Akufo-Addo.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-42) The court case generated considerable controversy, and was finally decided by the Ghana Supreme Court in a narrow 5/4 decision in favour of Mahama. Akufo-Addo accepted the verdict in the interest of economic stability and international goodwill.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-New_African-20)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-44)

In March 2014, Akufo-Addo announced his decision to seek his party's nomination for the third time ahead of the [2016 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Ghanaian_general_election "2016 Ghanaian general election"). In the NPP primary conducted in October 2014, he was declared victor with 94.35% of the votes.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-Afb-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-46) Akufo-Addo also served as chair of the Commonwealth Observer Mission for the South African elections in 2014.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-49)

He focused his campaign on the economy, promising to stabilize the country's foreign exchange rate and to reduce unemployment levels.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-50) On 9 December 2016, sitting president Mahama conceded defeat to Akufo-Addo.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-53) Akufo-Addo won the election with 53.83% of the votes against Mahama's 44.4%.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-55)

Akufo-Addo announced his intention to run for re-election by picking a nomination form as flagbearer of the New Patriotic Party ahead of the 2020 general elections.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-gbcghanaonline.com-56) On 9 December 2020, Akufo-Addo was declared the winner of the 7 December election after securing a majority of 51.59% of the vote, just enough to win re-election in a single round.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-nanare-elected-9)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-58) In December 2021, Akufo-Addo pledged to respect the two-term limit mandated in the [Ghanaian constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Ghana "Constitution of Ghana") and not run for a third term in 2024.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-59)

## President of Ghana (2017–2025)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: President of Ghana (2017–2025)")]

Further information: [Presidency of Nana Akufo-Addo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Nana_Akufo-Addo "Presidency of Nana Akufo-Addo")

### Inauguration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Inauguration")]

Akufo-Addo took office on 7 January 2017. His inauguration was held at [Black Star Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Star_Square "Black Star Square") in [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra"). Twelve presidents from African and [European countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_and_dependent_territories_in_Europe "List of sovereign states and dependent territories in Europe") attended the ceremony, including [Edgar Lungu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Lungu "Edgar Lungu") of [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia"), [Abdel Fattah el-Sisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdel_Fattah_el-Sisi "Abdel Fattah el-Sisi") of Egypt, [Ernest Bai Koroma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Bai_Koroma "Ernest Bai Koroma") of [Sierra Leone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Leone "Sierra Leone"), [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") of [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"), [Muhammadu Buhari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammadu_Buhari "Muhammadu Buhari") of Nigeria.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-62)

Akufo-Addo faced backlash, especially on social media, for plagiarizing parts of his inauguration speech, having lifted passages, word-for-word, from previous inaugural addresses given by American presidents [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy"), [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") and [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") as well as prepared remarks given by [Nigerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerians "Nigerians") President [Muhammadu Buhari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammadu_Buhari "Muhammadu Buhari") at a 2015 [United States Institute of Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Institute_of_Peace "United States Institute of Peace") event.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-68) After the scandal came to light, his press office issued an apology, with his communication director describing the situation as a "complete oversight and never deliberate."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-71) However, after the [mea culpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mea_culpa "Mea culpa"), it was found that Akufo-Addo had also plagiarized portions of his 2013 concession speech after the [Supreme Court of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Ghana "Supreme Court of Ghana") upheld the 2012 electoral victory of President [John Mahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama "John Dramani Mahama"). In that speech, lines were lifted verbatim from United States Vice-president [Al Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore "Al Gore")'s 2000 presidential concession speech given after the [US Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Supreme_Court "US Supreme Court") verdict.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-74)

### Education sector

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Education sector")]

In September 2017, Akufo-Addo launched the [Free Senior High School (SHS) policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_SHS "Free SHS"), which will make [secondary high school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_school "Secondary school") free for students in [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana"). The president states it is a "necessary investment in the nation's future workforce" and will help parents who are unable to pay for their children's education due to financial hardships. The program met with positive reaction from the nation, parents and students were excited and fervent, but private schools opposed to the program state it will decrease the number of students enrolling in their system.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-76)

In August 2023, Akufo-Addo cited the 2022 WASSCE success as proof of his education policies' effectiveness.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-:0-77) During a speech at Queen Girls Senior High School in the Western North region, the President credited last year's WASSCE results, the best in eight years, to the success of the Free Senior High School program and related initiatives.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-78) Akufo-Addo celebrated notable improvements in the 2022 WASSCE results, with higher scores in English, Integrated Science, Mathematics, and Social Studies. He also commended the 2021 student cohort for adapting to the double track system.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-:0-77)

### Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Economy")]

In 2018, the president introduced the 7-year Co-ordinated Programme of Economic and Social Development Policies which is expected to create jobs for the country. According to the president, the policies are founded on "five pillars of growth and development, namely revitalizing the economy; transform [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture") and industry; revamping economic and social infrastructure; strengthening social protection and inclusion; and reforming delivery system of public services institutions.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-79) Despite the [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") already warning the country that it was at high risk of debt-distress, the government of Akufo-Addo kept on borrowing, pushing up the nation's public debt from 56% of GDP to 63% before the pandemic. After the pandemic, Ghana borrowed even more in comparison with its neighbours, precipitating a budget-deficit crisis, the second highest in [Sub Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa") at 16% as of 2020, far above the regional average of 6%.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-80)

### LGBT rights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: LGBT rights")]

Akufo-Addo has taken a relatively moderate line on [LGBT rights in Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_Ghana "LGBT rights in Ghana"). In November 2017, he suggested that the legalisation of [homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality "Homosexuality") is inevitable and said he can foresee a change in the law.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-81) Akufo-Addo, who spent much of his early life in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"), said that LGBT rights will evolve in Ghana as they have in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). However, he affirmed that LGBT rights were not part of the government agenda at the moment.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-82) In August 2018, he reiterated that the [Government of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Ghana "Government of Ghana") would not legalise [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage "Same-sex marriage") or [decriminalise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decriminalization "Decriminalization") homosexuality under his leadership.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-84)

In February 2019, Akufo-Addo's administration announced a complete renovation of sports buildings around Ghana due to the country hosting the [African Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Games "African Games") in 2024. ### Other ventures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Other ventures")]

In 2019, the number of regions in Ghana increased from ten to sixteen under the president's administration. The new regions are [Oti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oti_Region "Oti Region"), [Western North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_North_Region "Western North Region"), [North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_Region,_Ghana "North East Region, Ghana"), [Ahafo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahafo_Region "Ahafo Region") (splitting from Brong), [Savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah_Region "Savannah Region") and [Bono East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bono_Region "Bono Region") Regions. The creation of the regions ends decades of petitions to the government calling for the development of new regions.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-86)

In 2020, he signed the [UNAIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNAIDS "UNAIDS") Public Letter on People's Vaccine which was a campaign calling for accessibility of the [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_disease_2019 "Coronavirus disease 2019") vaccine to all. He joined other world leaders in the signing. He wrote "all people everywhere must have access to the vaccine when one becomes available." Concerns were raised that people in richer countries may have quicker access to the vaccine than poor countries which led to the writing of an open letter that any vaccine against the disease should be free and made available at no cost to all people.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-citinewsroom.com-3) In February 2021, Ghana became the first African country to receive COVID-19 vaccines through the [World Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization")'s COVAX program. The shipment consisted of 600,000 doses of the [AstraZeneca vaccines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford%E2%80%93AstraZeneca_COVID-19_vaccine "Oxford–AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-87)

In May 2020, he swore into office two appointed [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Ghana "Supreme Court of Ghana") Judges, [Issifu Omoro Tanko Amadu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Issifu_Omoro_Tanko_Amadu "Issifu Omoro Tanko Amadu") and [Clemence Jackson Honyenuga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemence_Jackson_Honyenuga "Clemence Jackson Honyenuga") at the [Jubilee House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubilee_House "Jubilee House").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-89)

## Personal life

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/65/First_Lady_Melania_Trump%27s_Visit_to_Africa_%2843267916670%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Lady_Melania_Trump's_Visit_to_Africa_(43267916670)_(cropped).jpg)

 Akufo-Addo's third and current wife, [Rebecca Akufo-Addo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Akufo-Addo "Rebecca Akufo-Addo")

Akufo-Addo is from [Akropong-Akuapem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akropong-Akuapem "Akropong-Akuapem") and [Kyebi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyebi "Kyebi") in the [Eastern Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Region_(Ghana) "Eastern Region (Ghana)") and both sides of his family are [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_(USA) "Presbyterian Church (USA)").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-91) He is married to [Rebecca Akufo-Addo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Akufo-Addo "Rebecca Akufo-Addo") (née Griffiths-Randolph), the daughter of judge [Jacob Hackenburg Griffiths-Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Hackenburg_Griffiths-Randolph "Jacob Hackenburg Griffiths-Randolph"), the Speaker of the [Parliament of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Ghana "Parliament of Ghana") during the Third Republic.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-About_the_NPP:_Nana_Addo_Danquah_Akuffo-Addo-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-93) ,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-94) He was married to Eleanor Nkansah-Gyamenah,which the marriage ended on her death in 1993.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-95)

Akufo-Addo has four biological daughters and one stepdaughter: Gyankroma, Edwina, Adriana, Yeboakua and Valerie.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-97)[Virginia Hesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Hesse "Virginia Hesse") is the mother of one of his daughters.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-98) She was appointed by Akufo-Addo as Ghana's Ambassador to the [Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic "Czech Republic") in his first term.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-99) His first marriage to Remi bore him two of his daughters and his second marriage to Eleanor bore him a daughter.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-100) His marriage to Rebecca provided him a step-daughter had by Rebecca in a previous relationship.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-101) Akufo-Addo has a sister called Madam Marigold with the title, Abrewatia Nana Abena Oye.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-102)

Akufo-Addo is a [teetotaller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teetotaller "Teetotaller").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-104) An avid football fan, he is a supporter of [Asante Kotoko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asante_Kotoko_S.C. "Asante Kotoko S.C."), [Real Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Madrid_CF "Real Madrid CF"), and [Tottenham Hotspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur_F.C. "Tottenham Hotspur F.C.").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-106)

## Honours

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Honours")]

### Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nana_Akufo-Addo&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Awards")]

Akufo-Addo was presented with the [Mother Teresa Memorial International Award for Social Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_Teresa_Awards "Mother Teresa Awards") in 2016 by the Harmony Foundation for sacrificing political ambitions for the sake of national peace and reconciliation.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-107)

In May 2016, Akufo-Addo was bestowed Honorary Doctor of Law Degree from Fort Hare [University of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_South_Africa "University of South Africa"), recognizing his legal and political leadership.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-108)

In 2017, he received the National Achievement Award by the [Africa-America Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa-America_Institute "Africa-America Institute")'s on behalf of the people of Ghana. The award was given to recognise Ghana as a country that represents freedom, democracy and stability in Africa.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-109)

Almost a year into his Presidency in December 2017, Akufo-Addo received an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters degree from the [University of Liberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Liberia "University of Liberia").[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-110)

Akufo-Addo was given an award for Exemplary Leadership in June 2018, by the [Whitaker Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosa_Whitaker "Rosa Whitaker").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-112) In August 2018 he received the African Port Award by The African Port Award (APA) Foundation for his projects on modernizing Ghana's ports.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-113) In September 2018, the U.S. Africa Business Centre of the [United States Chamber of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Chamber_of_Commerce "United States Chamber of Commerce") presented Akufo-Addo with the 2018 Outstanding Leader's Award in recognition of regional, diplomatic, and economic leadership in Africa.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-114)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-115)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-116) In October 2018, he received the 2018 Governance Leadership Award "in recognition of his commitment towards enhancing the living standards of the Ghanaians and governing the country in accordance with the rule of law".[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-117)

In May 2019, the United Nations Secretary-General [António Guterres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Guterres "António Guterres") named Akufo-Addo among the newly appointed SDG advocates as co-chair alongside the prime minister of [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"), [Erna Solberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erna_Solberg "Erna Solberg").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-118) The role of these advocates is to raise awareness, inspire greater ambition, and push for faster action on the [Sustainable Development Goals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_Development_Goals "Sustainable Development Goals") (SDGs).

In June 2019, the [Association of National Olympic Committees of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_National_Olympic_Committees_of_Africa "Association of National Olympic Committees of Africa") (ANOCA) announced it will honour Akufo-Addo with the Association of National Olympic Committees of Africa (ANOCA) Merit Award for Heads of State due to his tremendous contribution to sports development and projects in Ghana and for the successful bid for Ghana to host the 2023 African Games.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-119)

Nana Akufo-Addo was honoured at the fourth Ghana Hotels Association Awards, held on 20 January 2020, for demonstrating visionary leadership by declaring the year of return and ensuring its successful execution.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-gbcghanaonline.com-56)

In May 2021, at a Congregation held in his honour, the University of Cape Coast conferred honorary Doctor of Philosophy in Educational Leadership degree on Akufo-Addo. The honorary degree, which is the highest honour given by the University, recognised his contribution to education in the country.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-120)

On 10 October 2022, the [University of Sorbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sorbonne "University of Sorbonne") in Paris, France presented an honorary doctorate degree to Akufo-Addo.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-121)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-122) Sorbonne recognized his commitment to democracy in Ghana, peace in West Africa, and his leadership in implementing the Free SHS policy and combating COVID-19.

On 8 August 2023, Akufo-Addo was presented with a Medal of Merit in Leadership Award by the African Bar Association.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-123)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-124)

In July 2024, Akufo-Addo received two honorary Doctorate degrees from two Universities in Ghana. On 14 July, Valley View University conferred honorary Doctorate on Akufo-Addo for his contribution to education and socio-economic development in Ghana and the sub-region as well as his unwavering desire to build an educated populace in the country.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-125) A fortnight later, the University of Health and Allied Sciences also honored Akufo-Addo with a Doctorate degree for his commitment to infrastructure development of the University and for the advancement of Science Education in the country.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-126)

On 6 November 2024, a statue was unveiled in his honour at the Effia-Nkwanta Regional Hospital in the Western Region, for the initiatives he has embarked on in the region during his term of office as indicated by the Western Regional Minister, Kwabena Okyere Darko.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-127)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-128)

In April 2026, Akufo-Addo was honoured by Otumfuo Osei Tutu II at the Asantehene's 27th enstoolment anniversary gala at Manhyia Palace, where he received a commemorative gold coin in recognition of his role in resolving long-standing chieftaincy and land disputes.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo#cite_note-129)

## #### World Cancer Day

Tuesday, 4th February, 2025  
[Hansard 4th February, 2025](https://www.parliament.gh/members?mp=94207) | [Read full Statement & Comments](https://www.parliament.gh/floor?dis=9)

Mr Speaker, thank you very much. I am Frank Yeboah, the Hon Member for Atwima Nwabiagya North.   
  
I want to add my voice to the Statement ably made by my Colleague, the Hon Member for Nsuta/Kwaman Beposo. We all agree that cancer is one of the killer diseases in the country and in the world at large.   
  
Mr Speaker, on the 23rd of December 2024, World Health Organization (WHO), released a report that sought to suggest that about 75 per cent of deaths globally are accounted for by non-communicable diseases, of which cancer is one. So, if we look at it, cancer is one of the killer diseases.   
  
In Ghana, the NHIS covers cervical cancer and breast cancer. Now, the NHIS also covers four main childhood cancers. But the unfortunate aspect is that it does not cover prostate cancer which is killing most men. Most men are suffering from prostate cancer, but unfortunately, we do not have any means of healthcare for that.   
  
Mr Speaker, I urge the House to cause prostate cancer treatment to be included in the NHIS benefit package so that men would not die and the workforce of the economy of the country would not die.   
  
Mr Speaker, thank you very much.   
  
  

## #### International Mother Language Day

Friday, 21st February, 2025  
[Hansard 21st February, 2025](https://www.parliament.gh/members?mp=94207) | [Read full Statement & Comments](https://www.parliament.gh/floor?dis=57)

Mr Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity to contribute to this important discussion on the occasion of International Mother Language Day. This day, observed globally on 21st February, serves as a reminder of the urgent need to preserve and promote linguistic diversity. In Ghana, where we are blessed with over 80 indigenous languages, this occasion presents an opportunity to reaffirm our commitment to safeguarding our linguistic heritage for future generations.   
  
Mr Speaker, language is not merely a tool for communication; it is the foundation of culture, identity, and historical continuity. Our indigenous languages carry the wisdom, traditions, and world views of our ancestors, shaping our understanding of ourselves and our communities. Yet, according to the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS), in 2023, many of these languages are under threat of extinction due to the pressures of urbanisation, globalisation, and the increasing dominance of English language in education and media.   
  
Mr Speaker, according to United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s (UNESCO), Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger 2021, several Ghanaian languages are classified as endangered, with a declining number of native speakers. Many young Ghanaians today struggle to communicate fluently in their mother tongues due to lack of formal education in these languages and the growing preference for English language in social and professional settings. This trend, if left unchecked, could result in the extinction of some of our rich languages.   
  
Mr Speaker, Ghana’s language policy on education has seen frequent shifts over the years. The current policy mandates the use of local languages as the medium of instruction from kindergarten to primary three before transitioning to English language. However, its implementation has been inconsistent, partly due to the limited availability of learning materials and trained teachers proficient in indigenous languages.   
  
Mr Speaker, the Bureau of Ghana Languages (BGL), established in 1951, has played a pivotal role in promoting and preserving Ghanaian languages through publications, translations, and language development programmes. However, the Bureau faces significant challenges, including understaffing, inadequate funding, and lack of modern technological resources. If we, as representatives of the people, are serious about preserving our indigenous languages, this institution must be adequately resourced to fulfil its mandate effectively.   
  
Mr Speaker, beyond Government’s efforts, the role of community engagement, digital technology, and media, cannot be overlooked. Promoting indigenous languages on radio, television, and social media platforms can help sustain their relevance among young people. Additionally, initiatives such as oral history documentation, digital dictionaries, and language-learning applications must be encouraged to bridge the intergenerational linguistic gap.   
  
Mr Speaker, I urge this House to support the Government to:   
a) Strengthen the Bureau of Ghana Languages (BGL) by increasing funding and technical support for its language development programmes.   
b) Ensure full implementation of the language-in-education policy by investing in teaching materials and training teachers in indigenous languages.   
c) Encourage the integration of indigenous languages in technology and media, ensuring they remain relevant in the digital age.   
d) Promote community-led language preservation programmes, including storytelling, oral history documentation, and intergenerational language transition initiatives.   
  
Mr Speaker, we cannot afford to lose our indigenous languages, for in them lies the heart and soul of our identity as Ghanaians. Let us act now to protect and promote them, ensuring that future generations inherit not just the words but the history, values, and wisdom they carry.   
  
Mr Speaker, I thank you once again for the opportunity.

**John Dramani Mahama** ([/m ə ˈ h ɑː m ə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/90/En-us-John_Dramani_Mahama_from_Ghana_pronunciation_%28Voice_of_America%29.ogg/En-us-John_Dramani_Mahama_from_Ghana_pronunciation_%28Voice_of_America%29.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-us-John_Dramani_Mahama_from_Ghana_pronunciation_(Voice_of_America).ogg "File:En-us-John Dramani Mahama from Ghana pronunciation (Voice of America).ogg"); born 29 November 1958)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-1) is a Ghanaian politician who has been the [president of the Republic of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Ghana "President of Ghana") since January 2025. A member of the [National Democratic Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Congress_(Ghana) "National Democratic Congress (Ghana)") (NDC), he previously served as president from 2012 to 2017.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-:1-3)

Mahama served as a Member of Parliament for [Bole/Bamboi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bole_(Ghana_parliament_constituency) "Bole (Ghana parliament constituency)") from 1997 to 2009 and served as [Deputy Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Minister "Deputy Minister") for Communication between 1997 and 1998 before becoming the substantive Minister for Communications in 1998.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-4) He then served as [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_Ghana "Vice President of Ghana") under President [John Atta Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Atta_Mills "John Atta Mills") from 2009 to 2012.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-:0-5) Mahama took office as president when Mills died in office on 24 July 2012.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-7) Mahama is the first vice president to assume the presidency following the death of his predecessor, and is the first head of state of Ghana to have been born after Ghana's independence in 1957.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-8)

He was elected in the [December 2012 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Ghanaian_general_election "2012 Ghanaian general election") to serve a full-term as president.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-autogenerated5-9) He contested re-election for a second term in the [2016 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Ghanaian_general_election "2016 Ghanaian general election") but lost to the [New Patriotic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Patriotic_Party "New Patriotic Party") candidate [Nana Akufo-Addo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo "Nana Akufo-Addo").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-10) This made him the first president in the history of Ghana to not have won a consecutive second term.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-:0-5) Mahama was again the NDC's presidential candidate in the [2020 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Ghanaian_general_election "2020 Ghanaian general election"), where he lost to Akufo-Addo.

He was re-elected president in the [2024 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Ghanaian_general_election "2024 Ghanaian general election"), defeating the then incumbent vice president [Mahamudu Bawumia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahamudu_Bawumia "Mahamudu Bawumia"), making him the first president in Ghanaian history to be democratically elected to a non-consecutive second term.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-11)

## Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Mahama&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early years")]

A member of the [Gonja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonja_people "Gonja people") ethnic group,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-13) Mahama hails from [Bole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bole,_Ghana "Bole, Ghana") in the [Savannah Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah_Region "Savannah Region") of Ghana. He was born on 29 November 1958 in [Damongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damongo "Damongo"), an area in the present-day [West Gonja District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Gonja_District "West Gonja District") of the [Northern Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Region_(Ghana) "Northern Region (Ghana)").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-14) His father, [Emmanuel Adama Mahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Adama_Mahama "Emmanuel Adama Mahama"), a wealthy rice farmer and teacher, was the first [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament "Member of Parliament") for the West Gonja constituency and the first Regional Commissioner of the Northern Region during the [First Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Republic_of_Ghana "First Republic of Ghana") under Ghana's first president, [Kwame Nkrumah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah "Kwame Nkrumah"). Mahama's father also served as a senior presidential advisor[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-15) during Ghana's [Third Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Republic_of_Ghana "Third Republic of Ghana") under [Hilla Limann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilla_Limann "Hilla Limann") who was [overthrown in 1981](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_Ghanaian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1981 Ghanaian coup d'état") by [Jerry John Rawlings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Rawlings "Jerry Rawlings").

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Mahama&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education")]

Mahama had his primary education at the [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra") Newtown Experimental School (ANT1) before going to boarding school at the [Achimota Primary School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achimota_School "Achimota School"). He completed secondary school, at [Ghana Secondary School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_Senior_High_School_(Tamale) "Ghana Senior High School (Tamale)"), in [Tamale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamale,_Ghana "Tamale, Ghana") a school in the Northern Region of Ghana. He proceeded to the [University of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana "University of Ghana"), [Legon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legon "Legon"), receiving a bachelor's degree in history in 1981 and a postgraduate diploma in communication studies in 1986. As a student, he was a member of [Commonwealth Hall Legon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Hall_Legon "Commonwealth Hall Legon"). He also studied at the Institute of Social Sciences in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") in the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), specializing in social psychology; he obtained a postgraduate degree in 1988.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-bio2-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-17)

## Early career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Mahama&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early career")]

After completing his undergraduate education, Mahama became a secondary school teacher for a few years.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-autogenerated2-18) Upon his return to [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana") after studying in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), he worked as the Information, Culture and Research Officer at the Embassy of Japan in [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra") between 1991 and 1995.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-autogenerated4-19) From there he moved to the anti-poverty [non-governmental organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organisation "Non-governmental organisation") (NGO) [Plan International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan_International "Plan International")'s Ghana Country Office, where he worked as International Relations, Sponsorship Communications and Grants Manager between 1995 and 1996.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-bio2-16) In 1993, he participated in a professional training course for Overseas Public Relations Staff, organized by the Japanese [Ministry of Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_(Japan) "Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Japan)") in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"). He also participated in a management development course organized by Plan International (RESA) in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"), Kenya.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-autogenerated3-20)

### As Member of Parliament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Mahama&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: As Member of Parliament")]

Mahama was first elected to the [Parliament of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Ghana "Parliament of Ghana") in the 1996[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-britannica-21) elections to represent the Bole/Bamboi Constituency for a four-year term. In April 1997, Mahama was appointed Deputy Minister of Communications.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-22) He was promoted to the post of Minister of Communications in November 1998, serving in that post until January 2001, when the ruling [National Democratic Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Congress_(Ghana) "National Democratic Congress (Ghana)") (NDC) handed over power to the [New Patriotic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Patriotic_Party "New Patriotic Party") government.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-bio-23)

In 2000, Mahama was re-elected for another four-year term as the Member of Parliament for Bole/Bamboi Constituency. He was again re-elected in 2004 for a third term. From 2001 to 2004, Mahama served as the Minority Parliamentary Spokesman for Communications. In 2002, he was appointed the Director of Communications for the NDC. That same year, he served as a member of the team of International Observers selected to monitor [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe")'s Parliamentary Elections.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-bio2-16) As an MP, he was a member of Standing Orders Committee as well as the Transport, Industry, Energy, Communications, Science and Technology Committee of Parliament.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-autogenerated6-24)

## As Minister and Vice Presidency (1997–2012)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Mahama&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: As Minister and Vice Presidency (1997–2012)")]

Mahama served as the Deputy Minister of Communications between April 1997 and November 1998. During his tenure as Minister for Communications, Mahama also served as the Chairman of the National Communications Authority, in which capacity he played a key role in stabilising Ghana's telecommunications sector after it was deregulated in 1997. As a minister, he was a founding member of the [Ghana AIDS Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_AIDS_Commission "Ghana AIDS Commission"), a member of the implementation committee of the 2000 National Population Census and a deputy chairman of the Publicity Committee for the re-introduction of the [Value Added Tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_Added_Tax "Value Added Tax") (VAT).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-John_Dramani_Mahama-26)

In 2003, Mahama became a member of the [Pan-African Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-African_Parliament "Pan-African Parliament"), serving as the Chairperson of the West African Caucus until 2011. He was also a member of European and Pan African Parliaments' Ad hoc Committee on Cooperation. In 2005, Mahama became the Minority Spokesperson for Foreign Affairs. He is a member of the [UNDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNDP "UNDP") Advisory Committee on [Conflict Resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_Resolution "Conflict Resolution") in Ghana.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-autogenerated3-20)

On 7 January 2009, Mahama was sworn into office as the Vice-President of Ghana with John Atta Mills as President.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-27) He also served as the Chairman of the National Economic Management Team, the [Armed Forces Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_Council "Armed Forces Council") of Ghana, the Decentralisation and Implementation Committee and the Police Council of Ghana in this capacity.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-:0-5)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-John_Dramani_Mahama-26)

## First presidency (2012–2017)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Mahama&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: First presidency (2012–2017)")]

Further information: [First presidency of John Mahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_John_Mahama "First presidency of John Mahama")

In line with [Ghana's constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Ghana "Constitution of Ghana"), Mahama became president on 24 July 2012 on the death of his predecessor, [John Atta Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Atta_Mills "John Atta Mills").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-28) In July 2012, he became Ghana's first president to have served at all levels of political office (Ghanaian and Pan-African MP, Deputy Minister, Minister, vice-president and President). He said in parliament upon being sworn in:

> This is the saddest day in our nation's history. Tears have engulfed our nation and we are deeply saddened and distraught and I'm personally devastated, I've lost a father, I've lost a friend, I've lost a mentor and a senior comrade. Ghana is united in grief at this time for our departed president.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-aljaz-29)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Secretary_Kerry_Meets_With_Ghanaian_President_Mahama_%289942939153%29.jpg/250px-Secretary_Kerry_Meets_With_Ghanaian_President_Mahama_%289942939153%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Secretary_Kerry_Meets_With_Ghanaian_President_Mahama_(9942939153).jpg)

John Mahama holds a [bilateral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilateralism "Bilateralism")[meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meeting "Meeting") with the then-[United States Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State")[John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry").

As a result of his elevation to the presidency, Mahama made political history by becoming the first [Ghanaian head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_heads_of_state_of_Ghana "List of heads of state of Ghana") to have been born after Ghana's [declaration of independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_independence "Declaration of independence") on 6 March 1957.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-30) The NDC held a Special National Delegates Congress on 30 August 2012 and endorsed Mahama as its 2012 presidential candidate. Mahama, the sole candidate of the party, polled 2,767 votes, representing 99.5% of total votes cast, to pick the slot for the party.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-ndc_endorses_president_mahama_as_2012_presidential_candidate-31) Mahama had stated that his administration was deeply committed to continuing the [Better Ghana Agenda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_Ghana_Agenda "Better Ghana Agenda") started under President Mills.

Mahama won the [December 2012 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Ghanaian_general_election "2012 Ghanaian general election") with 50.70% of the total valid votes cast and a 3% winning margin beating his nearest rival, [Nana Akufo-Addo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Akufo-Addo "Nana Akufo-Addo") of the main opposition [New Patriotic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Patriotic_Party "New Patriotic Party"), who polled a close 47.74%. This was just barely enough to win the presidency without the need for a runoff.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-autogenerated5-9) In addition, Mahama won the majority of valid votes cast in eight out of Ghana's ten administrative regions. Thirteen African Heads of State, one Prime Minister, two vice-presidents and 18 government delegations across the world attended his inaugural ceremony at the [Black Star Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Star_Square "Black Star Square") in [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra") on 7 January 2013, when Mahama was sworn in to begin his own four-year term.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-32)

After his investiture, the opposition New Patriotic Party led by Nana Akufo-Addo, his running mate, [Mahamudu Bawumia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahamudu_Bawumia "Mahamudu Bawumia") and the party chairman, [Jacob Otanka Obetsebi-Lamptey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Otanka_Obetsebi-Lamptey "Jacob Otanka Obetsebi-Lamptey"), challenged the election results, alleging irregularities, malpractices, omissions and violations. The petition was heard by nine justices of the [Supreme Court of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Ghana "Supreme Court of Ghana"). After eight months of hearing, the Court on 29 August 2013, dismissed the petition by a majority opinion.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-autogenerated6-24)

Mahama is one of Africa's most-followed leaders on the social networking sites, [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") and [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-33) In May 2013, he stated that all of West Africa is under the threat of [Islamist militancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamist_militancy "Islamist militancy").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dramani_Mahama#cite_note-34)
